messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mai, a 37-year-old refugee aid worker, was cycling through a crowded market in a border town when police vehicles surged into the square. She had been delivering food parcels to displaced families; within seconds, officers were swinging batons into the crowd. Her bicycle was knocked over, and she was trampled underfoot, pinned against a stall as people screamed and scattered. She remembers the terror and grief that overwhelmed her—crying for help that never came, feeling the weight of bodies pressing down. In the weeks that followed, she struggled to sleep, waking with her heart pounding, the same terror flooding back. She began to believe that what happened to her was deeply unfair and that nothing was ever done about it. That belief kept the memory alive; she would catch herself revisiting the trampling, searching for a point where someone—anyone—might have helped, as if the injustice had pinned her there in time. That conviction made her feel like she no longer knew herself; she started thinking, “Somebody else would not have let this happen,” though she could not say how they would have escaped. Once she had settled on the idea that she was weak and different, her attention began to snag on things that matched that story—a raised voice, a sudden crowd, the sight of a uniform—each one a potential confirmation of her new view of herself.

Now, every time Mai sees a police officer, the memory hits her with full force—the grief, the terror, the sense of being overwhelmed. These intrusions come so suddenly that she has to stop whatever she is doing, bracing herself against a wall. Because the memory arrived so vividly and without warning, she started to see its patterns everywhere: a bicycle propped by a lamppost, the sound of a whistle, the particular quality of late-afternoon light that reminded her of the market. She has learned to suppress the thoughts, pushing them down as hard as she can, but this only makes them stronger: a crowded sidewalk will suddenly become that market, and she will be back on the ground. On days when her body felt most on edge—her chest tight, her eyes scanning—the memory would surface as if the threat itself had conjured it, pulling her back into the trampling before she could brace. She also avoids situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful, because hope feels like a trap when injustice is everywhere. Never having let herself stay in a moment long enough to discover it was safe, her nervous system kept the threat level at the same pitch it had been that day, as if the avoidance itself proved the danger was still there. Her husband has noticed she no longer joins him for weekend walks near the park where cyclists pass; seeing people on bicycles triggers the same vivid memories, and she feels a surge of irritability, snapping at him before she can stop herself.

That irritability has bled into her work. As an aid worker, she still goes to crowded distribution sites, but she is increasingly reckless now—taking risks, volunteering for dangerous late-night supply runs because the adrenaline drowns out the memories. Yet those memories always return. When they do, the anger over the injustice resurfaces, and she spirals into gambling. She drives to a small card room two towns over, betting money she cannot afford to lose, distracting herself with the rush of the game. The gambling leaves her hollow, reinforcing her sense of identity loss: she used to be someone who cared, who believed in helping others. Now she feels like a stranger to herself. Her sleep has worsened; she lies awake replaying the event, the terror and grief washing over her until she gives up and scrolls through gambling sites on her phone.

Last month, Mai lost her temper with a volunteer driver after he mentioned that he rides a bicycle to work. She screamed at him, then walked away mid-shift. That outburst frightened her. It also made her realize that the memory is controlling her life—that every time she sees a police car, the injustice flares, and she ends up gambling or snapping. Her husband has said he feels helpless. What finally brought her to a therapist was the fear that she will lose her job and her marriage. She wants to stop the cycle, but she is terrified that facing the memory will break her completely. She hopes, somehow, to find the person she used to be—or at least to sleep through one night without the terror.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs about unfairness or weakness) directly cause or increase a sense of threat; the closest references link appraisals to attention or identity, not to perceived danger.

No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat directly drives maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, suppression, gambling); instead, maladaptive strategies are shown as responses to the memory or to negative appraisals, and threat is maintained by avoidance rather than triggered by it.
